paper.authors_full: Man ZHANG, Yang PENG, Yajie WANG, Huiqing HU, Shi CHEN, Qingbai ZHAO
paper.title: Perspective taking shapes creative performance in human-AI collaboration
paper.pdf_filename: Zhang et al (2026) - Perspective taking shapes creative performance in human-AI collaboration.pdf
paper.version_read: Undated 44-page English author manuscript headed Academic Paper for the 28th Annual Meeting of the China Association for Science and Technology (PDF p. 1). Its title-page note identifies an author-proofread translation of a Chinese original and says the Chinese version prevails. The supplied citation record identifies this saved file as PsyArXiv v1, 10.31234/osf.io/7x2v3_v1, published 2026-08-21, and distinguishes it from the later journal PDF; all estimates here use the saved manuscript.
paper.one_line_finding: Humans collaborating with GPT-5-mini generated more novel ideas than humans collaborating with another person in AUT (d = 0.47, p = 0.029; p. 17, section 3.2.2) and PIT (d = 0.42, p = 0.045; p. 22, section 3.3.2).
paper.shared_samples: No reuse of another paper's participants is stated. AUT and PIT are two tasks in this same experiment, not independent samples or separate studies.

studies.label: Laboratory collaboration experiment: alternative uses and product improvement

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 1, Abstract (randomized people); PDF p. 15, Table 1, human arm counts in column headings
counts_source.quote:
This study employed a between-subjects experimental design with a sample of 169 university students, who were randomly assigned to either the human−human collaboration or human−AI collaboration groups.
HAI (55) HH (114)

arms.name: Human in HAI
arms.description: Human collaborating with GPT–5–mini through a custom turn-taking chat interface, with the human speaking first. One human per HAI dyad. Table 1, PDF p. 15, prints HAI (55) before task-specific exclusions. The unique human count analyzed across both tasks is not printed.

arms.name: Human in HH
arms.description: Human collaborating with another human, without AI, through the same turn-taking chat interface. Each HH dyad comprises two humans. Table 1, PDF p. 15, prints HH (114) before task-specific exclusions. The unique human count analyzed across both tasks is not printed.

studies.task: The same students generated alternative uses for a rubber band (AUT; divergent_test) and creative improvements to a chair (PIT; idea_generation), alternating ideas with a human or AI partner in randomly ordered tasks.

ai_tool.name: GPT–5–mini
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 9, section 2.2: model named and API calls dated 2025/11/8 to 2025/12/21; release year is not stated.

preregistration.where: No preregistration is identified in the manuscript or appended supplement.

estimates.outcome: AUT: mean idea novelty (human-only role contrast)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Two graduate students with creativity research backgrounds independently rated each idea using the Consensual Assessment Technique on a seven-point scale, blind to condition, identities, and hypotheses; rater scores were averaged (PDF p. 13, section 2.5). Each person's score is the average across that person's own ideas.

open_items: The unique number of analyzed humans across the two tasks, and the corresponding human arm counts, are not printed. The task-specific totals are 155 for AUT and 164 for PIT (PDF p. 8). Table 2 prints 49 HAI and 53 HH dyads; Table 4 prints 54 HAI and 55 HH dyads. These are not entered as human arm counts and no totals are calculated from them.

Tables 2 and 4 do not identify the parenthetical dispersion values as SDs or SEs. Those values remain in verbatim source rows; SD, SE, and sd_level fields remain null. The weighting of member-level novelty/usefulness into dyad means is also unstated.

Exact human-only arm means, dispersion values, confidence intervals, and the standardizer for printed d effects are not specified. Exact human-pair t and d statistics are absent for the nonsignificant contrasts.

The exact random-effects and residual specifications for the unadjusted individual-role comparisons are not separately stated; dyad random intercepts are explicitly described for the APIM (PDF pp. 13-15). For whole-dyad t tests the observation unit is known to be team, but the se_basis vocabulary has no team category. These are individually assigned participants subsequently collaborating in dyads, so neither pair (two outputs compared) nor randomized-cluster precision is established by that design description. Whole-dyad records use unclear and preserve the paper's raw tests.

PIT human-only usefulness has only an overall three-role p value, not a reported human-pair contrast. The unreported contrast is listed in not_extracted; the omnibus p value is not substituted for a pairwise result (PDF p. 22).

Supplementary Figure 1 does not print exact forward-flow arm summaries, analyzed counts, test statistics, effect sizes, semantic model, distance algorithm, analysis unit, aggregation rule, or error-bar definition. All numerical fields in those figure-only records are null; graphical significance annotations are described only in notes.

The saved English translation is an earlier author manuscript according to the supplied citation record, not the later journal PDF. The document itself provides no version date and says that the Chinese original prevails. Extraction here is from the specified saved PDF only.
GPT–5–mini is named and its API-use dates are printed, but a release year is not stated; ai_tool.year is null.

The PIT delayed perspective-taking human contrast is described as nonsignificant in the Results and marginally significant in the Discussion; no additional exact statistic is supplied (PDF pp. 22 and 29).
